Etymology tree

Proto-Germanic *kaisarazder.
Proto-Slavic *cěsařь

Old East Slavic цьсарь (cĭsarĭ)

English czar
See tsar. The spelling czar, the older spelling in English, comes from the book Notes on Muscovite Affairs (1549) by Sigismund von Herberstein. It was supplanted by the alternative tsar in the 19th century.

s.d: a male monarch or emperor (especially of Russia prior to 1917)
(US, informal) An appointed official tasked to regulate or oversee a specific area.
a piece of music composed for the Hungarian Csárdás dance.
x: The Csárdás is characterized by a variation in tempo: it starts out slowly (lassú) and ends in a very fast tempo (friss, literally ‘fresh’).

s.d: a piece of music in the rhythm of the Hungarian Csárdás dance.
x: Classical composers who have used csárdás themes in their works include Emmerich Kálmán, Franz Liszt, Johannes Brahms, Léo Delibes, Johann Strauss, Pablo de Sarasate, Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky and others.

s.d: the wife or widow of a czar
of or relating to or characteristic of a czar

a Polish mead, made using three units of water for each unit of honey.
